arXiv:2104.03389v1 [math.AP] 07 Apr 2021

Indirect Stability of a multidimensional coupled wave equations with one locally boundary fractional damping

Mohammad AKIL1 and Ali Wehbe2
1Université Savoie Mont Blanc, Laboratoire LAMA, Chambéry-France.
2Lebanese University, Faculty of sciences 1, Khawarizmi Laboratory of Mathematics and Applications-KALMA, Hadath-Beirut.
Email: mohammad.akil@univ-smb.fr, ali.wehbe@ul.edu.lb
Abstract.

In this work, we consider a system of multidimensional wave equations coupled by velocities with one localized fractional boundary damping. First, using a general criteria of Arendt- Batty, by assuming that the boundary control region satisfy some geometric conditions, under the equality speed propagation and the coupling parameter of the two equations is small enough, we show the strong stability of our system in the absence of the compactness of the resolvent. Our system is not uniformly stable in general since it is the case of the interval. Hence, we look for a polynomial decay rate for smooth initial data for our system by applying a frequency domain approach combining with a multiplier method. Indeed, by assuming that the boundary control region satisfy some geometric conditions and the waves propagate with equal speed and the coupling parameter term is small enough, we establish a polynomial energy decay rate for smooth solutions, which depends on the order of the fractional derivative.

1. Introduction

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded domain of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, d≥2d\geq 2, with a Lipschitz boundary Γ=Γ0∪Γ1\Gamma=\Gamma_{0}\cup\Gamma_{1}, with Γ0\Gamma_{0} and Γ1\Gamma_{1} open subsets of Γ\Gamma such that Γ0¯∩Γ1¯=∅\overline{\Gamma_{0}}\cap\overline{\Gamma_{1}}=\emptyset and Γ1\Gamma_{1} is non empty. We consider the multidimensional coupled wave equations

(1.1) ut​t−Δ​u+b​yt\displaystyle u_{tt}-\Delta u+by_{t} =\displaystyle= 0,inΩ×(0,+∞),\displaystyle 0,\quad\text{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,+\infty),
(1.2) yt​t−a​Δ​y−b​ut\displaystyle y_{tt}-a\Delta y-bu_{t} =\displaystyle= 0,inΩ×(0,+∞),\displaystyle 0,\quad\text{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,+\infty),
(1.3) u\displaystyle u =\displaystyle= 0,onΓ0×(0,+∞),\displaystyle 0,\quad\text{on}\quad\Gamma_{0}\times(0,+\infty),
(1.4) y\displaystyle y =\displaystyle= 0,onΓ×(0,+∞),\displaystyle 0,\quad\text{on}\quad\Gamma\times(0,+\infty),
(1.5) ∂u∂ν+γ​∂tα,ηu\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}+\gamma\partial_{t}^{\alpha,\eta}u =\displaystyle= 0,onΓ1×(0,+∞),\displaystyle 0,\quad\text{on}\quad\Gamma_{1}\times(0,+\infty),

where ν\nu is the unit outward normal vector along the boundary Γ1\Gamma_{1}, γ\gamma is a positive constant involved in the boundary control, a>0a>0 and b∈ℝ∗b\in\mathbb{R}_{\ast}. The notation ∂tα,η\partial_{t}^{\alpha,\eta} stands the generalized Caputo’s fractional derivative see [17] of order α\alpha with respect to the time variable and is defined by

(1.6) [Dα,η​ω]​(t)=∂tα,ηω⁡(t)=1Γ⁡(1−α)​∫0t(t−s)−α​e−η⁡(t−s)​d​ωd​s​(s)​𝑑s, 0<α<1,η≥0.[D^{\alpha,\eta}\omega](t)=\partial_{t}^{\alpha,\eta}\omega(t)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)^{-\alpha}e^{-\eta(t-s)}\frac{d\omega}{ds}(s)ds,\ \ 0<\alpha<1,\ \eta\geq 0.

The system (1.1)-(1.5) is considered with initial conditions

(1.7) u​(x,0)=u0​(x),\displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x), ut​(x,0)=u1​(x)\displaystyle u_{t}(x,0)=u_{1}(x) wherex∈Ω,\displaystyle\text{where}\quad x\in\Omega,
(1.8) y​(x,0)=y0​(x),\displaystyle y(x,0)=y_{0}(x), yt​(x,0)=y1​(x)\displaystyle y_{t}(x,0)=y_{1}(x) wherex∈Ω,\displaystyle\text{where}\quad x\in\Omega,

The fractional derivative operator of order α\alpha, 0<α<10<\alpha<1, is defined by

(1.9) [Dα​f]​(t)=∫0t(t−τ)−αΓ⁡(1−α)​d​fd​τ​(τ)​𝑑τ.[D^{\alpha}f](t)=\int_{0}^{t}\dfrac{(t-\tau)^{-\alpha}}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\dfrac{df}{d\tau}(\tau)d\tau.

The boundary fractional damping of the type ∂tα,ηu\partial_{t}^{\alpha,\eta}u where 0<α<10<\alpha<1, η≥0\eta\geq 0 arising from the material property has been used in several applications such as in physical, chemical, biological, ecological phenomena. For more details we refer the readers to [27], [28], [10], [11], [12] and [26]. In theoretical point of view, fractional derivatives involves singular and non-integrable kernels (t−αt^{-\alpha}, 0<α<10<\alpha<1). This leads to substantial mathematical difficulties since all the previous methods developed for convolution terms with regular and/or integrable kernels are no longer valid.
There are a few numbers of publications concerning the stabilization of a distributed system with fractional damping. In [27], B. Mbodje considered a 1−d1-d wave equation with boundary fractional damping acting on a part of the boundary of the domain:

(1.10) {∂t2u⁡(x,t)−∂x2u⁡(x,t)=0,0<x<1,t>0,u⁡(0,t)=0.∂xu⁡(1,t)=−γ∂tα,ηu(1,t),0<α<1,η≥0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),∂tu⁡(x,0)=v0​(x),\left\{\begin{array}[]{rllll}\partial_{t}^{2}u(x,t)-\partial_{x}^{2}u(x,t)&=&0,&0<x<1,&t>0,\\ u(0,t)&=&0.&&\\ \partial_{x}u(1,t)&=&-\gamma\partial_{t}^{\alpha,\eta}u(1,t),&0<\alpha<1,&\eta\geq 0,\\ u(x,0)&=&u_{0}(x),&&\\ \partial_{t}u(x,0)&=&v_{0}(x),\end{array}\right.

Firstly, he proved that system (1.10) is not uniformly stable, on other words its energy has no exponential decay rate. However, using LaSalle’s invariance principle, he proved that system (1.10) is strongly stable for the usual initial data. Secondly, he established a polynomial energy decay rate of type 1t\frac{1}{t} for smooth initial data. In [3], Akil and wehbe considered a multidimensional wave equation with boundary fractional damping acting on a part of the boundary of the domain:

(1.11) {ut​t−Δ​u=0,inΩ×ℝ+,u=0,onΓ0×ℝ+,∂u∂ν+γ​∂tα,ηu=0,onΓ1×ℝ+,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)inΩ,ut​(x,0)=u1​(x),inΩ.\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllll}u_{tt}-\Delta u&=&0,&\text{in}&\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{+},\\ u&=&0,&\text{on}&\Gamma_{0}\times\mathbb{R}^{+},\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}+\gamma\partial_{t}^{\alpha,\eta}u&=&0,&\text{on}&\Gamma_{1}\times\mathbb{R}^{+},\\ u(x,0)&=&u_{0}(x)&\text{in}&\Omega,\\ u_{t}(x,0)&=&u_{1}(x),&\text{in}&\Omega.\end{array}\right.

Firstly, combining general criteria of Arendt and Batty with Holmgren’s theorem we showed the strong stability of system (1.11) in the absence of the compactness of the resolvent and without any additional geometric conditions. Next, the authors showed that their system is not uniformly stable in general, since it is the case of the interval. Hence, we look for a polynomial decay rate for smooth initial data for our system by applying a frequency domain approach combining with a multiplier method. Indeed, by assuming that the boundary control region satisfy the Geometric Control Condition (GCC) and by using the exponential decay of the wave equation with a standard damping

∂νu⁡(x,t)+ut​(x,t)=0,onγ1×ℝ+∗\partial_{\nu}u(x,t)+u_{t}(x,t)=0,\quad\text{on}\quad\gamma_{1}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\ast}

they established a polynomial energy decay rate for smooth solutions, which depends on the order of the fractional derivative (t−11−αt^{-\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}). In [18], Zhang and Dai considered the multidimensional wave equation with boundary source term and fractional dissipation defined by

(1.12) {ut​t−Δ​u=0,x∈Ωt>0,u=0,x∈Γ0t>0,∂u∂μ+∂tαu=|u|m−1​u,x∈Γ1t>0,u⁡(x,0)=u0,x∈Ω,ut​(x,0)=u1​(x),x∈Ω\left\{\begin{array}[]{rllll}u_{tt}-\Delta u&=&0,&x\in\Omega&t>0,\\ u&=&0,&x\in\Gamma_{0}&t>0,\\ \displaystyle{\frac{\partial u}{\partial\mu}+\partial_{t}^{\alpha}u}&=&|u|^{m-1}u,&x\in\Gamma_{1}&t>0,\\ u(x,0)&=&u_{0},&x\in\Omega,&\\ u_{t}(x,0)&=&u_{1}(x),&x\in\Omega&\end{array}\right.

where m>1m>1. They proved by Fourier transforms and the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality the exponential stability for sufficiently large initial data.
In [1], Benaissa and al. considered the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation with boundary dissipation of fractional derivative type defined by

(1.13) {φt​t​(x,t)+φx​x​x​x​(x,t)=0,in]0,L[×]0,+∞[,φ⁡(0,t)=φx​(0,t)=0,in]0,+∞[,φx​x​(L,t)=0,in]0,+∞,φx​x​x​(L,t)=γ​∂tα,ηφ⁡(L,t),in]0,+∞[\left\{\begin{array}[]{rllll}\varphi_{tt}(x,t)+\varphi_{xxxx}(x,t)&=&0,&\text{in}&]0,L[\times]0,+\infty[,\\ \varphi(0,t)=\varphi_{x}(0,t)&=&0,&\text{in}&]0,+\infty[,\\ \varphi_{xx}(L,t)&=&0,&\text{in}&]0,+\infty,\\ \varphi_{xxx}(L,t)&=&\gamma\partial_{t}^{\alpha,\eta}\varphi(L,t),&\text{in}&]0,+\infty[\end{array}\right.

where 0<α<10<\alpha<1, η≥0\eta\geq 0 and γ>0\gamma>0. If η=0\eta=0, by using spectral analysis, they proved the non-uniform stability. Otherwise, if η>0\eta>0, they proved that the energy of system (1.13) decay as time goes to infinity as 1t11−α\frac{1}{t^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}}.
In [4] see also ([5]-[6]), Alabau-Boussouira studied the boundary indirect stabilization of a system of two-level second order evolution equations coupled through the zero-order terms. The lack of uniform stability as proved in the case where the ratio of the wave propagation speeds of the two equation is equal to 1k2\frac{1}{k^{2}} with kk being an integer and Ω\Omega is a cubic domain in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, or by a compact perturbation argument and a polynomial energy decay rate of type 1t\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}} is obtained by a general integral inequality in the case where the wave propagates at the same speed and Ω\Omega is a star-shaped domain in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}. These results are very interesting but not optimal.
In [8], Ammari and Mehrenberger gave a characterization of the stability of a system of two evolution equations coupling through the velocity terms subject one bounded viscous feedbacks.
In [23] Liu and Rao, considered a system of two coupled wave equations with one boundary damping described by

(1.14) {ut​t−a​Δ​u+α​y=0,inΩ×ℝ+,yt​t−Δ​y+α​u=0,inΩ×ℝ+,a​∂νu+γ​u+ut=0,onΓ1×ℝ+,u=0,onΓ0×ℝ+,y=0,onΓ×ℝ+\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllll}u_{tt}-a\Delta u+\alpha y&=&0,&\text{in}&\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{+},\\ y_{tt}-\Delta y+\alpha u&=&0,&\text{in}&\Omega\times\mathbb{R}^{+},\\ a\partial_{\nu}u+\gamma u+u_{t}&=&0,&\text{on}&\Gamma_{1}\times\mathbb{R}^{+},\\ u&=&0,&\text{on}&\Gamma_{0}\times\mathbb{R}^{+},\\ y&=&0,&\text{on}&\Gamma\times\mathbb{R}^{+}\end{array}\right.

Under some arithmetic condition on the ratio of the wave propagation speeds of the two equations, they established a polynomial energy decay rate for smooth initial data on a 1-dimensional domain. Furthermore, under the equality speed wave propagation, they proved that the energy of the system (1.14) decays at the rate 1t\frac{1}{t} for smooth initial data on an N−N-dimensional domain Ω\Omega with the usual geometrical condition.

In [7] Ammar-Khodja and Bader studied the simultaneous boundary stabilization of a system of two wave equations coupling through the velocity terms described by

(1.15) {ut​t−ux​x+b⁡(x)​yt=0,in(0,1)×(0,+∞),yt​t−a​yx​x−b⁡(x)​ut=0,in(0,1)×(0,+∞),yt​(0,t)−α⁡(yx​(0,t)+ut​(0,t))=0,in(0,+∞),ux​(0,t)−α​yt​(0,t)=0,in(0,+∞),u⁡(1,t)=y⁡(1,t)=0,in(0,+∞)\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllll}u_{tt}-u_{xx}+b(x)y_{t}&=&0,&\text{in}&(0,1)\times(0,+\infty),\\ y_{tt}-ay_{xx}-b(x)u_{t}&=&0,&\text{in}&(0,1)\times(0,+\infty),\\ y_{t}(0,t)-\alpha\left(y_{x}(0,t)+u_{t}(0,t)\right)&=&0,&\text{in}&(0,+\infty),\\ u_{x}(0,t)-\alpha y_{t}(0,t)&=&0,&\text{in}&(0,+\infty),\\ u(1,t)=y(1,t)&=&0,&\text{in}&(0,+\infty)\end{array}\right.

where aa and α\alpha are two constants strictly positives and b∈𝒞0​([0,1])b\in{\mathcal{C}}^{0}\left([0,1]\right). In the general case, when a≠1a\neq 1, they proved that the system (1.15) is uniformly stable if and only if it is strongly stable and there exists integer numbers pp and qq such that a=(2​p+1)2q2a=\frac{(2p+1)^{2}}{q^{2}}. Otherwise, under the equal speed wave propagation condition (i.e. a=1a=1), they proved that the system (1.15) is uniformly stable if and only if it is strongly stable and the coupling parameter b⁡(x)b(x) verifies that ∫01b⁡(x)​𝑑x≠(2​k+1)​π2\int_{0}^{1}b(x)dx\neq\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2} for any k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}. Note that, system (1.15) is damped by two related boundary controls.
In [2], Akil, Ghader and Wehbe considered a 1−d1-d coupled wave equations on its indirect boundary stabilization defined by:

(1.16) {ut​t−ux​x+b​yt=0,in(0,1)×ℝ+∗,yt​t−a​yx​x−b​ut=0,in(0,1)×ℝ+∗,ux​(1,t)+γ​∂tα,ηy⁡(1,t)=0,inℝ+∗,u⁡(0,t)=y⁡(0,t)=y⁡(1,t)=0,inℝ+∗,\left\{\begin{array}[]{lllll}u_{tt}-u_{xx}+by_{t}&=&0,&\text{in}&(0,1)\times\mathbb{R}^{\ast}_{+},\\ y_{tt}-ay_{xx}-bu_{t}&=&0,&\text{in}&(0,1)\times\mathbb{R}^{\ast}_{+},\\ u_{x}(1,t)+\gamma\partial_{t}^{\alpha,\eta}y(1,t)&=&0,&\text{in}&\mathbb{R}^{\ast}_{+},\\ u(0,t)=y(0,t)=y(1,t)&=&0,&\text{in}&\mathbb{R}^{\ast}_{+},\end{array}\right.

where a>0a>0 and b∈ℝ∗b\in\mathbb{R}^{\ast}. Firstly, they proved that system (1.16) is strongly stable if and only if the coupling parameter bb is outside a discrete set SS of exceptional values. Next, for b∉Sb\notin S, they proved that the energy decay rate of system (1.16) is greatly influenced by the nature of the coupling parameter bb (an additional condition on bb) and by the arithmetic property of the ratio of the wave propagation speeds aa. They established a polynomial energy decay rate of type t−s⁡(α)t^{-s(\alpha)}, such that

  1. (1)

    If a=1a=1 and b≠k​πb\neq k\pi, then s⁡(α)=21−αs(\alpha)=\frac{2}{1-\alpha}.

  2. (2)

    If (a=1a=1 and b=k​πb=k\pi), or (a≠1a\neq 1, a∈ℚa\in\mathbb{Q}, a∉ℚ\sqrt{a}\notin\mathbb{Q} and bb small enough), or (a≠1a\neq 1 and a∈ℚ\sqrt{a}\in\mathbb{Q}) or (a≠1a\neq 1 and for almost a∈ℝ/ℚ\sqrt{a}\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Q}), then s⁡(α)=25−αs(\alpha)=\frac{2}{5-\alpha}.

The polynomial energy decay rate occurs in many control problems where the open-loop systems are strongly stable, but not exponentially stable (see [19]). We quote [20], [21] for wave equations with local internal or boundary damping, [13] and [22] for abstract system, [30] and [32] for systems of coupled wave-heat equations.
This paper is organized as follows: In Subsection 2.1, we reformulate the system (1.1)-(1.8) into an augmented model system by coupling the wave equation with a suitable equation and we prove the well-posedness of our system by semigroup approach. In subsection 2.2, under the equal speed wave propagation condition (i.e. a=1a=1) and if the coupling parameter bb is small enough, using a general criteria of Arendt-Batty theorem, we show that the strong stability of our system for in the absence of the compactness of the resolvent and under the multiplier geometric control condition noted by (MGC). In Section 3, under the equal speed wave propagation and the coupling parameter bb verify another condition, we look for a polynomial decay rate for smooth initial data for our system by applying a frequency domain approach combining with a multiplier method. Indeed, by assuming that the boundary control region satisfy (MGC) boundary condition, we establish a polynomial energy decay for smooth solution of type 1t21−α\frac{1}{t^{\frac{2}{1-\alpha}}}.

2. Well-Posedness and Strong Stability

In this section, we will study the strong stability of system (1.1)-(1.8) in the absence of the compactness of the resolvent and by the (MGC) condition. First, we will study the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of the system of our system.

2.1. Augmented model and well-Posedness

which leads to the well-posedness of (2.18). Hence, we have the following result.

Theorem 2.4.

For any U0∈ℋU_{0}\in\mathcal{H}, problem (2.18) admits a unique weak solution

U⁡(t)∈C0​(ℝ+,ℋ).U(t)\in C^{0}(\mathbb{R}^{+};\mathcal{H}).

Moreover, if U0∈D⁡(𝒜)U_{0}\in D(\mathcal{A}), then

U⁡(t)∈C1​(ℝ+,ℋ)∩C0​(ℝ+,D⁡(𝒜)).U(t)\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{+},\mathcal{H})\cap C^{0}(\mathbb{R}^{+},D(\mathcal{A})).

2.2. Strong Stability in case a=1a=1

In this subsection, under the condition of equality of speed propagation wave (i.e. a=1a=1), the coupling parameter term bb is small enough and the boundary satisfies the (MGC) boundary condition, we study the strong stability of system (2.3)-(2.11) in the sense that its energy converges to zero when tt goes to infinity for all initial data in ℋ\mathcal{H} . First, we introduce here the notions of stability that we encounter in this work and the definition of the boundary multiplier geometric conditions denoted by (MGC).

Definition 2.5.

Assume that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the generator of a C0−C_{0}-semigroup of contractions (et​𝒜)t≥0\left(e^{t\mathcal{A}}\right)_{t\geq 0} on a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}. The C0−C_{0}-semigroup (et​𝒜)t≥0\left(e^{t\mathcal{A}}\right)_{t\geq 0} is said to be

  1. 1.1.

    strongly stable if

    limt→+∞‖et​𝒜​x0‖ℋ=0,∀x0∈ℋ;\lim_{t\to+\infty}\|e^{t\mathcal{A}}x_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=0,\quad\forall\ x_{0}\in\mathcal{H};
  2. 2.2.

    exponentially (or uniformly) stable if there exist two positive constants MM and ϵ\epsilon such that

    ‖et​𝒜​x0‖ℋ≤M​e−ϵ​t​‖x0‖ℋ,∀t>0,∀x0∈ℋ;\|e^{t\mathcal{A}}x_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq Me^{-\epsilon t}\|x_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}},\quad\forall t>0,\ \forall x_{0}\in\mathcal{H};
  3. 3.3.

    polynomially stable if there exists two positive constants CC and α\alpha such that

    ‖et​𝒜​x0‖ℋ≤C​t−ℓ​‖𝒜​x0‖ℋ,∀t>0,∀x0∈D⁡(𝒜).\|e^{t\mathcal{A}}x_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq Ct^{-\ell}\|\mathcal{A}x_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}},\quad\forall t>0,\quad\forall x_{0}\in D\left(\mathcal{A}\right).

    In that case, one says that conditions of (2.18) decays at t−ℓt^{-\ell}. The C0−C_{0}-semigroup (et​𝒜)t≥0\left(e^{t\mathcal{A}}\right)_{t\geq 0} is said to be polynomially stable with optimal decay rate t−ℓt^{-\ell} (with ℓ>0\ell>0) if it is polynomially stable with decay rate t−ℓt^{-\ell} and, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough, there exists solutions of (2.18) which do not decay at a rate t−(ℓ−ε)t^{-(\ell-\varepsilon)}

In fact, since the resolvent of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not compact, then the classical methods such as Lasalle’s invariance principle [31] or the spectrum decomposition theory of Benchimol [15] are not applicable. In this case, we use a general criteria of Arendt-Batty [9]. We will rely on the following result obtained by Arendt and Batty.

Theorem 2.6.

(Arendt and Batty in [9]) Assume that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the generator of a C0−C_{0}-semigroup of contractions (et​𝒜)t≥0\left(e^{t\mathcal{A}}\right)_{t\geq 0} on a Hilbert space HH. If

  1. 1.1.

    𝒜\mathcal{A} has no pure imaginary eigenvalues,

  2. 2.2.

    σ⁡(𝒜)∩i​ℝ\sigma(\mathcal{A})\cap i\mathbb{R} is countable,

where σ⁡(𝒜)\sigma(\mathcal{A}) denotes the spectrum of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, then the C0−C_{0}-semigroup (et​𝒜)t≥0\left(e^{t\mathcal{A}}\right)_{t\geq 0} is strongly stable.

Definition 2.7.

(MGC) We say that the boundary Γ\Gamma satisfies the boundary multiplier geometric control condition (MGC) if there exists x0∈ℝdx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a positive constant m0>0m_{0}>0 such that

m⋅ν≤0onΓ0andm⋅ν≥m0onΓ1m\cdot\nu\leq 0\ \ \text{on}\ \ \Gamma_{0}\quad\text{and}\quad m\cdot\nu\geq m_{0}\ \ \text{on}\ \ \Gamma_{1}

with m⁡(x)=x−x0m(x)=x-x_{0}, for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Our main result in this part is the following theorem.

Theorem 2.8.

Suppose that η≥0\eta\geq 0, a=1a=1, bb small enough and Γ\Gamma satisfies (MGC), then the C0−C_{0}-semigroup (et​𝒜)t≥0(e^{t\mathcal{A}})_{t\geq 0} is strongly stable on the energy space ℋ\mathcal{H} in the sense that limt→+∞‖et​𝒜​U0‖ℋ=0\displaystyle{\lim_{t\rightarrow+\infty}\|e^{t\mathcal{A}}U_{0}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=0} for all U0∈ℋU_{0}\in\mathcal{H}.

3. Polynomial Stability

In this section, we use the frequency domain approach method combining with multiplier method in the case that η>0,a=1,b\eta>0,\ a=1,b small enough and under the (MGC) condition defined in Definition 2.7, with Γ0¯∩Γ¯1=∅\overline{\Gamma_{0}}\cap\overline{\Gamma}_{1}=\emptyset. The frequency domain approach method has been obtained by Batty in [13]-[14], Borichev and Tomilov in [16] and Liu and Rao in [22].

    supλ∈ℝ‖(i​λ​I−𝒜)−1‖ℒ⁡(ℋ)=O⁡(|λ|ℓ)\displaystyle{\sup_{{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}}\left\|\left(i{\lambda}I-\mathcal{A}\right)^{-1}\right\|_{\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}\right)}}=O\left(\lvert{\lambda}\rvert^{\ell}\right),

    ‖et​𝒜​U0‖ℋ≤Ct1ℓ∀t>0,U0∈D⁡(𝒜),for some​C>0\left\|e^{t\mathcal{A}}U_{0}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\frac{C}{t^{\frac{1}{\ell}}}\quad\forall t>0,\ U_{0}\in D(\mathcal{A}),\ \text{for some}\ C>0.

Proof of Theorem 3.2. Using (3.33), (3.45) and (3.48), we get

(3.69) ∫Ω|∇u|2dx=o(1),∫Ω|λy|2dx=o(1),and∫Ω|∇y|2dx=o(1).\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}dx=o(1),\ \ \int_{\Omega}|{\lambda}y|^{2}dx=o(1),\ \ \text{and}\ \ \int_{\Omega}|\nabla y|^{2}dx=o(1).

It follows from (3.10), (3.48) and (3.69), that ‖U‖ℋ=o⁡(1)\|U\|_{\mathcal{H}}=o(1) which contradicts (3.3). Consequently condition (H3){\rm(H3)} holds and the energy of smooth solution of system (2.3)-(2.11) decays polynomial to zero as tt goes to infinity where a=1a=1 and bb small enough. In view of the asymptotic behaviour of the eigenvalues of the operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} (see proposition 2.14 ), we conjecture that the energy decay rate of type t−21−αt^{-\frac{2}{1-\alpha}} is optimal (see [25]). The proof has been completed.

Conclusion

We studied the stabilization of multidimensional coupled wave equations via velocities with one locally boundary fractional damping acting on a part of the boundary of the domain. First, under the (MGC) boundary condition without, the strong stability is proved if a=1a=1 and the coupling parameter term is small enough. Next, under the (MGC){\rm(MGC)} boundary condition with Γ0¯∩Γ1¯=∅\overline{\Gamma_{0}}\cap\overline{\Gamma_{1}}=\emptyset a polynomial energy decay rate of type 1t21−α\frac{1}{t^{\frac{2}{1-\alpha}}} is established if a=1a=1 and the coupling parameter term is small enough. Moreover, it would be interesting to

  1. (1)

    study the strong stability of system (1.1)-(1.8) in case that a≠1a\neq 1, bb is not necessarily small enough and without any additional geometric boundary control condition,

  2. (2)

    generalize the results obtained in [2] (see system (1.16)) to the multidimensional case.

M2​(α,d)=γ​k​(α,d)​∫0+∞ρ2​α−11+η+ρ2​(∏j=1d−2(∫0πsind−1−j⁡(ϕj)​d​ϕj)​∫02​πd​ϕd−1)​𝑑ρ.M_{2}(\alpha,d)=\gamma k(\alpha,d)\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{\rho^{2\alpha-1}}{1+\eta+\rho^{2}}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{d-2}\left(\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin^{d-1-j}(\phi_{j})d\phi_{j}\right)\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\phi_{d-1}\right)d\rho.

On the other hand, it is easy to see that

(4.3) ∏j=1d−2(∫0πsind−1−j⁡(ϕj)​d​ϕj)​∫02​πd​ϕd−1=d​πd2Γ⁡(d2+1).\prod_{j=1}^{d-2}\left(\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin^{d-1-j}(\phi_{j})d\phi_{j}\right)\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\phi_{d-1}=\frac{d\pi^{\frac{d}{2}}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}+1\right)}.

This implies that

M2​(α,d)=2​γ​sin⁡(α​π)π​∫0+∞ρ2​α−11+η+ρ2​𝑑ρ.M_{2}(\alpha,d)=2\frac{\gamma\sin(\alpha\pi)}{\pi}\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{\rho^{2\alpha-1}}{1+\eta+\rho^{2}}d\rho.

A direct computation gives

M2​(α,d)=γ​sin⁡(α​π)π​∫0+∞xα−11+η+x=γ​sin⁡(α​π)π​(1+η)α−1​∫01(1−z)α−1zα​𝑑z=γ​sin⁡(α​π)π​(1+η)α−1​Γ​(1−α)​Γ​(α)=γ​(1+η)α−1.\begin{array}[]{lllll}M_{2}(\alpha,d)&=&\displaystyle{\frac{\gamma\sin(\alpha\pi)}{\pi}\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{x^{\alpha-1}}{1+\eta+x}}\\ \\ &=&\displaystyle{\frac{\gamma\sin(\alpha\pi)}{\pi}(1+\eta)^{\alpha-1}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{(1-z)^{\alpha-1}}{z^{\alpha}}dz}\\ \\ &=&\displaystyle{\frac{\gamma\sin(\alpha\pi)}{\pi}\left(1+\eta\right)^{\alpha-1}\Gamma(1-\alpha)}\Gamma(\alpha)\\ \\ &=&\displaystyle{\gamma\left(1+\eta\right)^{\alpha-1}}.\end{array}

 □\square

Lemma 4.2.

Let η≥0\eta\geq 0, then we have

S1=∫ℝd|ξ|2​α−d+2(1+|ξ|2+η)2​𝑑ξ<+∞.S_{1}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\lvert\xi\rvert^{2\alpha-d+2}}{(1+\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}+\eta)^{2}}d\xi<+\infty.

S1=d​πd2Γ⁡(d2+1)​∫0+∞ρ2​α+1(1+η+ρ2)2​𝑑ρ.S_{1}=\frac{d\pi^{\frac{d}{2}}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}+1\right)}\int_{0}^{+\infty}\frac{\rho^{2\alpha+1}}{(1+\eta+\rho^{2})^{2}}d\rho.

Since, we have

ρ2​α+1(1+ρ2+η)2​∼0​ρ2​α+1(1+η)2andρ2​α+1(1+ρ2+η)2​∼+∞​1ρ3−2​α.\frac{\rho^{2\alpha+1}}{(1+\rho^{2}+\eta)^{2}}\underset{0}{\sim}\frac{\rho^{2\alpha+1}}{(1+\eta)^{2}}\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{\rho^{2\alpha+1}}{(1+\rho^{2}+\eta)^{2}}\underset{+\infty}{\sim}\frac{1}{\rho^{3-2\alpha}}.

Using the fact that α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), we get S1S_{1} is well defined.  □\square

Lemma 4.3.

Let η>0\eta>0 and d≥2d\geq 2, then we have

{B1:=∫ℝd|ξ|α+d2(|λ|+|ξ|2+η)d+1​𝑑ξ=c1​(α,d)​(|λ|+η)α2−d4−1,A2:=∫ℝd|ξ|2​d−2(|λ|+|ξ|2+η)2​d​d​ξ=c2​(d)​(|λ|+η)−1−d2,A3:=∫ℝd|ξ|2​d(|λ|+|ξ|2+η)2​d+2​dξ=c3​(d)​(|λ|+η)−d2−2.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\displaystyle{B_{1}:=\displaystyle{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\lvert\xi\rvert^{\alpha+\frac{d}{2}}}{\left(\lvert{\lambda}\rvert+|\xi|^{2}+\eta\right)^{d+1}}d\xi}=c_{1}(\alpha,d)\left(\lvert{\lambda}\rvert+\eta\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{d}{4}-1},}\par\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\cr\displaystyle{A_{2}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\lvert\xi\rvert^{2d-2}}{\left(\lvert{\lambda}\rvert+\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}+\eta\right)^{2d}d\xi}=c_{2}(d)\left(\lvert{\lambda}\rvert+\eta\right)^{-1-\frac{d}{2}},}\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\cr\displaystyle{A_{3}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\lvert\xi\rvert^{2d}}{\left(\lvert{\lambda}\rvert+\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}+\eta\right)^{2d+2}}d\xi=c_{3}(d)\left(\lvert{\lambda}\rvert+\eta\right)^{-\frac{d}{2}-2}}.\end{array}\right.

such that

Proof. Our first aim is to calculate B1B_{1}. Using the hyper-spherical coordinates and the fact that the Jacobian JJ defined in equation (4.2), we get
